newsitem.title: USA: Jenny Jones must testify in talk show murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Jenny Jones must testify in talk show murder trial.

text.p: Talk show host Jenny Jones is expected to testify Thursday in a Michigan murder trial after a judge ruled Wednesday she is a relevant witness to the defence of Jonathan Schmitz.

Schmitz, 26, is accused of first-degree murder in the shotgun death of Scott Amedure, 32, three days after Amedure revealed his affection for Schmitz during a taping of the "Jenny Jones" show on secret admirers.
Defence attorney James Burdick said he hoped to call Jones to the stand Thursday afternoon.
"She's going to have to explain why they did things the way they did and why she went out of her way for the sake of ratings to yank every last bit of emotion of Jon," Burdick said.
Jones' appearance as a witness was cleared by Oakland County Circuit Judge Francis O'Brien, who granted a defence motion that her testimony is relevant to Schmitz' defence.

Schmitz, who says he is not homosexual, alleges he was humiliated in front of the studio audience. That experience, combined with manic depression and Graves disease, a thyroid condition that can have emotional side effects, contributed to his buying a 12-guage shotgun and shooting Amedure twice in the chest on March 9, 1995, defence attorneys say.

O'Brien's ruling reversed an earlier decision that removed her from the witness list. The judge said Jones would be able to testify only to her personal knowledge, conduct and involvement before and during the show in which Schmitz appeared.
O'Brien said earlier testimony elicited from prosecutors opened the door for defence attorneys to add Jones to the witness list.
An attorney representing Telepictures, the unit of Warner Bros. that produces the "Jenny Jones" show, said he was not worried about Jones appearance.

"We're not at all concerned about it. We have long maintained that she should not be called to testify because she doesn't know anything of relevance to this case," said Mike Huget, attorney with Butzel Long in Detroit.
Prosecutors said Wednesday they believed the jury would be able to focus on the events in Michigan. A tape of the show was never aired on television, but was played for jurors in Schmitz' trial.
Court was recessed Wednesday but will resume Thursday. Jurors have heard 10 days of testimony since opening arguments were made on Oct. 14.

Although prosecutors have charged Schmitz with first-degree murder, the jury will also have the option of finding him guilty of second-degree murder, manslaughter, or reckless discharge causing death. If convicted of the most severe offence, Schmitz could be sentenced to life in prison without possibility of parole.
